A population of cells derived from a single cell is called a clone, and a clone is genetically identical. In general, plants retain "totipotency", the ability to differentiate into all the cells that make up an individual, even in the somatic cells of the adult, so in many cases clones can be produced from various somatic cells through the regeneration of individuals by tissue culture.

On the other hand, in higher animals such as mammals, only very limited cells, such as eggs and fertilised eggs, have "totipotency", so the production of clones is extremely difficult. The procedure by which Dolly, the world's first cloned sheep, announced in 1997, was produced was as follows.

Step 1: Mammary gland cells of a sheep of strain 1 are collected and cultured under special conditions.

Step 2: The nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg of a sheep of strain 2.

Step 3: The cells prepared in Step 1 and Step 2 are fused, and cells in which cleavage has started normally are placed in the uterus of a sheep of strain 3 to make it pregnant.

After many failures, Dolly was born. Choose from A–I the correct description of the genetic composition of Dolly. (3 points)

A. Completely genetically identical to the strain 1 sheep

B. Completely genetically identical to the strain 2 sheep

C. Completely genetically identical to the strain 3 sheep

D. Genetically almost identical to the strain 1 sheep, but with mitochondrial genes of the strain 2 sheep mixed in

E. Genetically almost identical to the strain 1 sheep, but with mitochondrial genes of the strain 3 sheep mixed in

F. Genetically almost identical to the strain 2 sheep, but with mitochondrial genes of the strain 1 sheep mixed in

G. Genetically almost identical to the strain 2 sheep, but with mitochondrial genes of the strain 3 sheep mixed in

H. Genetically almost identical to the strain 3 sheep, but with mitochondrial genes of the strain 1 sheep mixed in

I. Genetically almost identical to the strain 3 sheep, but with mitochondrial genes of the strain 2 sheep mixed in

During the development of the mammalian cerebral cortex, neural stem cells are present deep in the brain, and by their cell divisions they produce both neural stem cells themselves and neurons. To analyse the cell cycle of the neural stem cells, mouse embryos were used as a model and thymidine labelled with a radioactive isotope was administered to the mother mouse. The labelled thymidine passes through the placenta and is taken up by the neural stem cells of the embryo that are in the process of DNA synthesis. Because the labelled thymidine is constantly being metabolised, it was administered continuously. Taking the time at which the labelled thymidine was first administered as 0, if the proportion of cells that had incorporated labelled thymidine into their nuclear DNA among all the neural stem cells changed with time as in the figure below, what can be said about the cell cycle of the neural stem cells? Choose from A–I.

Assume, however, that the length of the cell cycle is the same in all the neural stem cells. Also, because the neurons produced by cell division immediately migrate and leave the observed site, the change in the size of the whole cell population at the observed site during the observation period can be ignored. In addition, cells that have incorporated even a small amount of labelled thymidine are counted as cells that have incorporated it. (3 points)

Using the PCR (polymerase chain reaction) method, species can be identified from their DNA to some extent. One of its applications is the identification of "aonori" (青のり, green laver). There are situations in which seaweeds of the genus Enteromorpha (アオノリ属) must be distinguished from those of the genus Ulva (アオサ属), which are used as their substitute. However, because the products are mainly in powdered form, it is difficult to distinguish the two by microscopic observation. If, therefore, a part of the base sequence specific to the genus Enteromorpha is amplified by PCR and checked by electrophoresis, they can easily be distinguished.

A certain "aonori" was tested by the following procedure, and the result below was obtained. In order to conclude that "this sample is not of the genus Enteromorpha", what is necessary in addition to this test? Choose the combination of correct ones from A–J. (3 points)

[Procedure and result]

(1) DNA is extracted from the sample.

(2) Primers corresponding to the base sequence specific to the genus Enteromorpha were added, and that part of the base sequence was amplified by PCR.

(3) This was checked by electrophoresis, but no band corresponding to that base sequence was seen.

[What is necessary in addition]

① Treat DNA known to be from the genus Enteromorpha in the same way and confirm that a band appears.

② Treat DNA known to be from the genus Enteromorpha in the same way and confirm that no band appears.

③ Treat DNA known to be from the genus Ulva in the same way and confirm that a band appears.

④ Treat DNA known to be from the genus Ulva in the same way and confirm that no band appears.

⑤ Treat DNA known to be from neither the genus Enteromorpha nor the genus Ulva in the same way and confirm that a band appears.

⑥ Treat DNA known to be from neither the genus Enteromorpha nor the genus Ulva in the same way and confirm that no band appears.

Rubisco (ルビスコ) is a carboxylase that works in carbon fixation in photosynthesis, and it catalyses the reaction (Reaction 1) in which two molecules of phosphoglycerate are synthesised from ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate and $\mathrm{CO_2}$. On the other hand, however, Rubisco also has oxygenase activity and also catalyses the reaction in which ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate combines with $\mathrm{O_2}$ (Reaction 2).

Reaction 1: ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate + $\mathrm{CO_2}$ + $\mathrm{H_2O}$ → 2 × phosphoglycerate

Reaction 2: ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate + $\mathrm{O_2}$ → phosphoglycerate + phosphoglycolate

Which reaction takes priority is determined by conditions such as the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ concentrations at the reaction site and the temperature. Of these, the effect of temperature is largely due to the property of Rubisco that "when the temperature rises, its affinity for $\mathrm{CO_2}$ falls markedly, but its affinity for $\mathrm{O_2}$ changes little".

Now let us consider another world, in which only the properties of plant Rubisco differ from those in the real world. In this hypothetical world, Rubisco is assumed to be such that "its affinity for $\mathrm{CO_2}$, like its affinity for $\mathrm{O_2}$, is not affected by temperature". In such a world, how would the distributions of C4 plants, which carry out C4 photosynthesis, and of CAM plants, which carry out crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM), compare with the real world? Considering how the environments in which C4 plants and CAM plants have an advantage over C3 plants, which carry out standard photosynthesis, change with the properties of Rubisco, infer the distributions of C4 plants and CAM plants in the hypothetical world and choose the most appropriate statement from A–I. (4 points)

A. The distributions of both C4 plants and CAM plants expand.

B. The distribution of C4 plants expands, but the distribution of CAM plants changes little.

C. The distribution of C4 plants expands, but the distribution of CAM plants shrinks.

D. The distribution of C4 plants changes little, but the distribution of CAM plants expands.

E. The distributions of both C4 plants and CAM plants change little.

F. The distribution of C4 plants changes little, but the distribution of CAM plants shrinks.

G. The distribution of C4 plants shrinks, but the distribution of CAM plants expands.

H. The distribution of C4 plants shrinks, but the distribution of CAM plants changes little.

I. The distributions of both C4 plants and CAM plants shrink.

Plants show a phenomenon called phototropism, in which they grow towards the direction of light, and it has long been known that the light causing phototropism is blue light. That an organism responds to light of a particular colour means nothing other than that it has a photoreceptor substance that selectively absorbs only light of that colour and causes a physiological phenomenon. About 15 years ago it became clear that what absorbs blue light and causes phototropism is a photoreceptor protein called phototropin. In plants, besides the photoreceptor substances working in photosynthesis, cryptochrome also exists as a blue-light-absorbing photoreceptor substance other than phototropin, so whether cryptochrome is also involved in regulating the direction of plant growth was examined using Arabidopsis (シロイヌナズナ), one of the higher plants.

Fifty Arabidopsis seeds were grown for 4 days in darkness (Figures 1–3, upper row) or under irradiation with blue light from above (Figures 1–3, lower row); the growth direction of the hypocotyl of the seedlings (the organ corresponding to the stem of the seedling) was measured, and the results were shown as histograms. Because the growth direction of the hypocotyl was measured as in Figure 4, 0 degrees represents growth vertically upwards, and −90 degrees and +90 degrees represent growth in horizontal directions. In addition to wild-type individuals (Figure 1), phototropin-deficient mutants (Figure 2) and cryptochrome-deficient mutants (Figure 3) were also examined.

Judging from the experimental results, choose the most appropriate combination of statements from A–I. (4 points)

In the senescence of leaves, which are photosynthetic organs, the equilibrium between the synthesis and degradation of chloroplast proteins, which is normally kept in balance, tilts towards degradation, so chlorophyll decreases and yellowing occurs. Leaves detached from the plant senesce rapidly when kept in the dark, but if cytokinin is given to the leaves at that time, senescence is suppressed. Also, in soybean, leaf senescence progresses as the seeds mature in autumn, but if the young pods (fruits) that grow after pollination are picked off one after another, leaf senescence is delayed. This leaf senescence is thought to be suppressed by cytokinin synthesised in the roots. Choose from A–H the combination of statements considered appropriate concerning experiments on senescence using soybean. Note that the liquid flowing in the xylem vessels is called xylem sap. Not a few climbing plants develop tendrils. Many tendrils are regarded as modified leaves, but there are also tendrils thought to be modified stems. To find out whether the tendrils of a certain climbing plant are a kind of leaf or a kind of stem, it was decided to observe their cells and tissues. In this observation, what information about the tendrils would be especially useful? Choose from A–E. (3 points)

A. Presence or absence of chloroplasts in the internal tissues

B. Presence or absence of stomata on the surface

C. Presence or absence of hairs on the surface

D. Branching pattern of the internal vascular bundles

E. Arrangement of xylem and phloem in cross-section

Planarians, which are flatworms (Platyhelminthes), have a high regenerative ability. The following is known about the regeneration of planarians.

(1) In the body of a normal planarian there is a group of cells that actively carry out DNA synthesis. These cells are called S cells.

(2) When an individual was irradiated with X-rays, which destroy cells with high proliferative ability, its S cells decreased.

(3) When the regeneration of the X-irradiated individuals was observed, they hardly regenerated.

From these findings, the hypothesis "S cells are, at least, stem cells necessary for regeneration" was put forward. Choose from A–F the most appropriate experiment needed to test this hypothesis further. (3 points)

A. Transplant part of the tissue of an X-irradiated individual into a normal individual and examine whether it has regenerative ability.

B. Transplant part of the tissue of a normal individual into an X-irradiated individual and examine whether its regenerative ability recovers.

C. Transplant part of the tissue of an X-irradiated individual into an X-irradiated individual and examine whether its regenerative ability recovers.

D. Transplant S cells of a normal individual into an X-irradiated individual and examine whether its regenerative ability recovers.

E. Transplant S cells of a normal individual into a normal individual and examine whether its regenerative ability changes.

F. Rear an X-irradiated individual for a long period and then examine whether its regenerative ability recovers.

The animal body is equipped with mechanisms that maintain the constancy of the internal environment (homeostasis) against changes in the external environment, and it has the ability to remain active without being greatly affected by environmental changes. The American physiologist Cannon (Cannon, W. B.) removed the sympathetic trunks of the right side of the thorax and abdomen of cats in order to examine the functions of the sympathetic nervous system in maintaining homeostasis. When these cats were placed in various environments and their responses were observed, the following results were obtained.

(1) When the sympathectomised cats were exposed to cold, the hair of the left half from the spine stood on end, but the hair of the right half did not.

(2) When the body temperature of the cats in the cold was recorded, results such as those in Figure a were obtained. The solid lines show the rectal temperature of the control group and the broken lines the rectal temperature of the sympathectomised group. The zigzags below each record show the intensity of the cats' shivering response.

(3) Control cats (3 cats) and sympathectomised cats (2 cats) were each given a stimulus of the same degree to provoke anger. Figure b shows the change in blood glucose level at this time and the record of the blood glucose level before the stimulus.

(4) Unless given special stimuli, the sympathectomised cats lived for more than 3 years in a healthy state in the stable environment of the laboratory without developing any notable impairment.

The black and yellow stripe pattern of the zebrafish is formed by the distribution of black pigment cells and yellow pigment cells. These pigment cells differentiate from common pigment stem cells, but which pigment cell they become is determined by influences from their surroundings. To examine the influence of existing pigment cells, the following experiments were therefore carried out using a method in which individual pigment cells are killed by burning and removed with microscopic laser irradiation. The experiments are shown schematically in the figure below.

Experiment 1: All the yellow pigment cells were removed in one area of a yellow stripe. Two weeks later, a few yellow pigment cells had appeared.

Experiment 2: All the yellow pigment cells were removed in one area of a yellow stripe. In addition, all the black pigment cells around it were removed. Two weeks later, a few yellow pigment cells and many black pigment cells had appeared in the part from which the yellow pigment cells had been removed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2011-1-14-fig1.png

In certain kinds of plants, flower-bud formation is induced depending on the maturation of the plant body through a certain growth period (age), in addition to environmental factors such as day length and low temperature. Recent research has made it clear that the substance of florigen (the flowering hormone that induces flowering), whose synthesis is promoted by such external and internal factors, is a protein called FT, and that it has various physiological functions besides the induction of flowering. In the poplar, a deciduous broad-leaved tree distributed from the temperate to the subarctic zone, flower-bud differentiation and bud dormancy are induced in response to the seasonal change in day length. An FT called PtFT also exists in this poplar. When poplars constitutively expressing the PtFT gene at a high level were produced using genetic engineering, flower buds were formed in only half a year, although normally many years are needed before flower buds come to be formed. On the other hand, the deciduous poplar (wild type) stops the growth of its buds (leaf buds) and forms dormant buds from the end of summer into autumn. Experiments were carried out to clarify the function of PtFT in the poplar, and the following results were obtained.

1. Expression of the PtFT gene was high from spring to early summer.

2. From the end of summer to autumn, the PtFT gene was not expressed.

Experiments using genetically modified poplars grown in a growth chamber

The formation of the limbs of birds has long been a subject of experimental embryology. The limbs of birds and mammals develop from limb buds (small swellings that give rise to the limbs) projecting from the trunk of the embryo; the limb bud elongates and bones and muscles are formed inside it. As for the bones, the forelimb (wing) of a bird has three digit bones, numbered II, III and IV from the anterior side (the thumb side in humans) (Figure 1). The following experiments were carried out on the mechanism that determines the anterior and posterior (the little-finger side in humans) of the bird forelimb.

Experiment 1: When the anterior region of a limb bud was transplanted into the posterior region of another limb bud, digit bones II, III and IV were formed in the limb bud, as in a normal wing.

Experiment 2: When the posterior region of a limb bud was transplanted into the anterior region of another limb bud, extra digit bones were formed; from the anterior side they were digit bones IV, III, II, III and IV (Figure 2). Of these, the anterior extra digits IV and III were not derived from the transplanted cells.

Experiment 3: Among the genes expressed only in the posterior region of the limb bud, when a gene called X was expressed in large amounts in the anterior region, the same result as with transplantation of the posterior region was obtained. The product of the X gene is a substance secreted outside the cell.

In most vertebrates, oocytes that have grown sufficiently in the ovary are arrested in prophase of the first meiotic division. These oocytes resume meiosis on hormonal stimulation, then arrest again at metaphase of the second meiotic division, and are ovulated as mature eggs (unfertilised eggs) to await fertilisation. This process is called oocyte maturation, and the existence of factors controlling the process of oocyte maturation was proposed from experiments using frogs. When cytoplasm of an unfertilised egg was injected into a blastomere of a 2-cell embryo, cleavage stopped at metaphase of the division. However, when cytoplasm of a fertilised egg was injected into a blastomere, cleavage did not stop and proceeded normally. On the other hand, when cytoplasm of an unfertilised egg was injected into an immature oocyte, oocyte maturation proceeded without hormonal stimulation and the oocyte became an unfertilised egg. Choose from A–E the most appropriate conclusion that can be drawn from the above experimental results. (4 points)

A. On hormonal stimulation, a factor that suppresses oocyte maturation is made in the cytoplasm of the oocyte, and it is broken down after fertilisation.

B. On hormonal stimulation, a factor that suppresses oocyte maturation and a factor that can arrest both the second meiotic division and somatic cell division at metaphase are made in the cytoplasm of the oocyte.

C. On hormonal stimulation, a factor that induces oocyte maturation and a factor that can arrest both the second meiotic division and somatic cell division at metaphase are made in the cytoplasm of the oocyte.

D. On hormonal stimulation, a factor that suppresses oocyte maturation and a factor that arrests the second meiotic division at metaphase but cannot arrest somatic cell division at metaphase are made in the cytoplasm of the oocyte.

E. On hormonal stimulation, a factor that induces oocyte maturation and a factor that arrests the second meiotic division at metaphase but cannot arrest somatic cell division at metaphase are made in the cytoplasm of the oocyte.

The nematode C. elegans has an XO-type mode of sex determination: XX becomes a hermaphrodite and XO becomes a male. The hermaphrodite makes both sperm and eggs itself and lays offspring produced by self-fertilisation. When a hermaphrodite is mated with a male, the eggs of the hermaphrodite are preferentially fertilised by sperm from the male.

In sex determination by sex chromosomes, a signal depending on the kind and number of sex chromosomes regulates the activity of several genes one after another and finally determines the sex-specific traits of the organism. These genes are called sex-determination genes, and when a mutation occurs in one of them, the mutant becomes one of the two sexes regardless of the kind and number of its sex chromosomes. Among the recessive mutations in the sex-determination genes of C. elegans, there is a mutation with which both XX and XO become males. The offspring obtained when an XX male homozygous for this mutation is crossed with a wild-type hermaphrodite (XX) are called F₁, and the offspring produced by self-fertilisation of the hermaphrodites among the F₁ are called F₂. What, then, are the sex ratio of F₁ (written p : q) and the sex ratio of F₂ (written r : s)? Compare them with the sex ratios obtained when the same experiment is carried out using a wild-type hermaphrodite and a wild-type male (XO), and choose the correct sex ratios from A–J. (4 points)

In eukaryotes, many examples are known in which microtubules, part of the cytoskeleton, are arranged regularly and used as organelles of cell movement. One of them, the flagellum, is seen in the sperm of animals, in the zoospores and sperm of some plants and fungi, and in many protists. However, angiosperms, the major fungi and some protists do not have flagella. Eukaryotic flagella basically have a common structure in which the microtubules are arranged 9 + 2, as in (a). In the ciliates, which belong to the protists, and in the epithelial cells of animals, many cilia grow from the cell and contribute to cell movement and the generation of water currents; basically, each individual cilium has the same 9 + 2 structure as in (a), like the flagellum.

The "axopodia" seen in the protist heliozoans and radiolarians are also structures formed by regularly arranged microtubules; they extend radially from the cell and contribute to the cell movement of protists, for example by shortening when capturing food. The structure of the axopodia differs greatly between species. (b) is a cross-section of an axopodium of the actinophryid heliozoans (無殻太陽虫類), in which the microtubules are arranged in a spiral. On the other hand, (c) is a cross-section of an axopodium of the centrohelid heliozoans (有中心粒太陽虫類), in which the microtubules are arranged in a combination of hexagons and triangles. As a result of molecular phylogenetic analysis, it is known that the actinophryid heliozoans and the centrohelid heliozoans, although similar in form, are phylogenetically far apart. Sea urchins of species X become blastulae 20 hours after fertilisation and begin gastrulation 5 hours after that. It is also known that, in both sea urchins, by immersing them once in seawater of low osmotic pressure and then returning them to normal seawater (hypotonic seawater treatment), even unfertilised eggs develop with the same time course as fertilised eggs. Experiments were carried out using these two species of sea urchin, and the following experimental results 1–6 were obtained.

1. When the nucleus was removed from unfertilised eggs of species X and hypotonic seawater treatment was carried out, they became blastulae 20 hours after the treatment, and development stopped there.

2. When the nucleus was removed from unfertilised eggs of species Y and hypotonic seawater treatment was carried out, they became blastulae 7 hours after the treatment, and development stopped there.

3. When unfertilised eggs of species X were fertilised with sperm of species Y, they became blastulae 20 hours after fertilisation and began gastrulation 5 hours after that.

4. When unfertilised eggs of species Y were fertilised with sperm of species X, they became blastulae 7 hours after fertilisation and began gastrulation 3 hours after that.

5. When the nucleus of a fertilised egg of species Y was transplanted into an enucleated unfertilised egg of species X and hypotonic seawater treatment was carried out, it became a blastula 20 hours after fertilisation and began gastrulation 3 hours after that.

Salamander larvae (at the stage at which the forelimbs and hindlimbs have come out) were anaesthetised and subjected to surgery to remove the pituitary gland, and its effects were examined. The experiment was carried out with 20 individuals divided into the following three groups.

Group (1): individuals that were anaesthetised and had the pituitary surgically removed (10 individuals)

Group (2): individuals that were anaesthetised and given a sham operation in which a scalpel was inserted to near the pituitary (5 individuals)

Group (3): individuals that were neither anaesthetised nor operated on (5 individuals)

The operated individuals behaved normally, without their health being impaired by the surgery. After the surgery they were reared for 2 months, with the following results. It is known that the body-colour changes of salamanders are caused by the aggregation and dispersion of the black pigment granules of the pigment cells of the body surface.

[I] When each group was observed 3 hours after the surgery, in 8 individuals of group (1) (called group 1-1) the body colour of the parts other than the tail had become lighter than in groups (2) and (3), and the remaining 2 individuals (called group 1-2) had become black. As for the colour tone of the tail, there was no difference among groups (1), (2) and (3).

[II] When they were exposed to bright illumination (light conditions), the individuals of group (1-1) and the individuals of groups (2) and (3) showed a light body colour and no difference could be seen, but the individuals of group (1-2) remained black in body colour.

[III] When they were placed in the dark, groups (2) and (3) showed a black body colour, and the individuals of group (1-1) remained light in body colour. The individuals of group (1-2) remained black in body colour.

[IV] When the individuals of groups (1), (2) and (3) were blindfolded under light conditions and left for a while, the same results as in [III] were obtained.

[V] Two months after the surgery, groups (2) and (3) had completed metamorphosis, but the 10 individuals of group (1) showed no sign of metamorphosis at all.

[VI] When the heads of the 10 individuals of group (1) were examined, in the individuals of group (1-1) no pituitary at all was found, while in the individuals of group (1-2) there was no tissue of the anterior lobe of the pituitary, and the intermediate lobe remained, separated from the diencephalon.

Adult toads (ヒキガエル) are completely terrestrial animals; they do not normally enter ponds or rivers, and they live mainly at night, crawling about on the ground and eating small animals, chiefly insects. To find out how toads find the pond in which they breed, several hypotheses were set up and an experiment was carried out.

[Hypotheses]

① They gather, attracted by the calls of the males heard from the pond. (The first males reach the pond by chance.)

② Because the toads begin their activity after sunset, they find the direction of the pond using the direction of the set sun as a cue.

③ They visually remember the route from the breeding pond.

④ They can sense the Earth's magnetic field lines (geomagnetism) and find the direction of the pond on that basis.

⑤ They remember the smell of the ground along their route.

⑥ They gather, attracted by some chemical substance in the pond water.

[Experiment] Many toads heading from east to west towards the breeding pond were captured, put in equal numbers into two boxes, and covered with black cloth so that they could not see outside. One box was carried to the west side and then back to the original position on the east side, where the toads were taken out of the box and released (control group); the other box was carried to the west side, and the toads were taken out of the box and released there (experimental group). When the subsequent behaviour of the toads was examined, most individuals of the control group again began to move towards the pond, but the experimental group did not try to move in a fixed direction, and each individual moved in a different direction.

The arrangement of leaves follows a regular pattern that is fixed for each plant. For example, in many plants that bear one leaf at each node, the angle made by successive leaves (with the stem as the centre) is constant at about 135–140°, and therefore the leaves form a neat spiral. Such regularity is thought to arise because, when a new leaf arises at the periphery of the shoot apical meristem, its position is determined under the influence of the preceding leaves. To investigate this influence, the following experiment was carried out using tomato.

Let the leaf that has only just begun to develop be called $\mathrm{I_1}$, the leaf that appears next $\mathrm{I_2}$, and the leaf after that $\mathrm{I_3}$. Species that have been carried by humans to regions where they do not originally occur and have spread there are called alien species. At present, many alien plant species have been reported, and some of them flourish vigorously in the areas they have invaded and have become a problem. In such alien plant species, abnormal flourishing is sometimes seen only in the invaded area and not in the native area. As an explanation of such a phenomenon, there is the idea that in the native area there are herbivores (natural enemies) that suppress the population growth of the plant, but they are absent from the area invaded by the alien species, so that an outbreak occurred. In that case, there is a prediction that, because the plant is released from its natural enemies in the invaded area, it stops defending itself against natural enemies; this is called the enemy release hypothesis. Furthermore, there is a prediction that the advantage arises that the energy saved by stopping defence can be invested in growth, and the alien species becomes stronger in competition with other plants. This is called the increased competitive ability hypothesis.

A researcher chose an alien plant species for which there was no large environmental difference between the native area and the invaded area other than the presence or absence of herbivores (natural enemies), and carried out a cultivation experiment using native-area lines and invaded-area lines. The cultivation experiment was carried out under a condition with natural enemies (natural enemies present) and a condition without them (natural enemies absent), and the amount of feeding damage, the amount of growth and the fitness were examined (figure below). In this plant species it was known that fitness is represented by the number of seeds, so the number of seeds produced during the cultivation period was taken as the fitness. The researcher concluded that differences in the properties predicted by the enemy release hypothesis and the increased competitive ability hypothesis have arisen between the native-area and invaded-area lines, and that these are very likely to have brought about adaptive differentiation.

The above conclusion consists of three elements: "there are differences predicted by the enemy release hypothesis", "there are differences predicted by the increased competitive ability hypothesis" and "these differences are adaptive differentiation". Of parts ①–⑥ of the figure, which parts did the researcher need to derive each element of the conclusion? Choose the most suitable combination from A–J. (4 points)

Skeletal muscle is a tissue made of bundles of giant cells called muscle fibres, and the muscle fibres contain bundles of myofibrils. A myofibril is a repetition of a unit structure called the sarcomere (Figure 1) and is the basic structure that brings about muscle contraction. The length of a typical skeletal-muscle sarcomere is about 2.5 µm. As shown in Figure 1, the actin filaments extending from the Z membrane (sometimes also called the Z line, Z band or Z disc) are about 1.0 µm long, and the myosin filaments are about 1.6 µm long. Because the myosin filaments interact with the actin filaments and act so as to pull the actin filaments in, the distance between the Z membranes becomes shorter as a result, and the whole muscle also contracts.

The tension per sarcomere is greater the more myosin heads interact with the actin filaments. However, the myosin heads that can interact with actin are present only on about 0.6 µm on each side of the myosin filament; the central approximately 0.4 µm has no myosin heads and therefore cannot react with actin. It is also known that when the sarcomere is stretched to about 4.0 µm so that the actin filaments and myosin filaments are separated, the interaction between the myosin heads and the actin filaments disappears, but because the two sides are connected by a weakly elastic protein, the original structure is restored when the pulling force is removed.

The compound eyes of insects arise from a group of cells called a primordium (compound-eye primordium) inside the body of the larva. Let $Q$ be the wild-type allele involved in the synthesis of the vermilion pigment, $q$ the recessive allele that has lost its function, $T$ the wild-type allele involved in the synthesis of the brown pigment and $t$ the recessive allele that has lost its function. Then with genotype $Qqtt$ or $QQtt$ the compound eyes are vermilion, with genotype $qqTt$ or $qqTT$ the compound eyes are brown, and with genotype $qqtt$ the compound eyes are white.

The bodies of many multicellular organisms are built on three axes: anterior–posterior, dorsal–ventral and left–right. In the fruit fly (ショウジョウバエ), the directions of the anterior–posterior axis and the dorsal–ventral axis are determined in early embryogenesis by concentration gradients of factors distributed unevenly within the embryo. Specifically, the direction of the anterior–posterior axis is determined by the action of factor α, which forms a concentration gradient from the anterior to the posterior of the embryo, and factor β, which forms a concentration gradient from the posterior to the anterior. On the other hand, the direction of the dorsal–ventral axis is determined by factor γ, which forms a concentration gradient from the ventral to the dorsal side. However, the mechanism that determines the direction of the third axis, the left–right axis, is not clear. A researcher therefore put forward the following two hypotheses.

Hypothesis 1: A factor separate from those that determine the directions of the anterior–posterior and dorsal–ventral axes exists, and its concentration gradient determines the direction of the left–right axis.

Hypothesis 2: The direction of the left–right axis is determined depending on the directions of the anterior–posterior and dorsal–ventral axes.

To test these hypotheses, the effect on the direction of the left–right axis of completely reversing only the direction of the anterior–posterior axis was examined. First, to reverse the direction of the anterior–posterior axis completely, factor α and factor β were artificially exchanged (reversed embryo). In this case the position of the micropyle in the eggshell does not change, so the original anterior–posterior direction and the anterior–posterior direction of the reversed embryo can be judged independently. Next, these reversed embryos were used to judge which hypothesis is correct. The direction of the left–right axis was judged from the way the gut, which is formed by the late stage of embryogenesis, curves.

The ratio of the amount of CO₂ released by an organism through respiration to the amount of O₂ it absorbs (CO₂/O₂) is called the respiratory quotient (RQ). For gases, regardless of the molecular species, equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules at a given pressure and temperature. Therefore, the RQ can be obtained by measuring the volume ratio of CO₂ to O₂ at a given pressure and temperature.

Suppose that a human eats only glucose (grape sugar, C₆H₁₂O₆) as the metabolic substrate and metabolises it completely. In this case, by passing through glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain (including oxidative phosphorylation), one molecule of glucose becomes six molecules of carbon dioxide and six molecules of water. Since six molecules of oxygen are consumed in this process, RQ = 1. Because the ratio of O₂ consumed to CO₂ released is expected to differ when the metabolic substrate differs, the diet can be inferred by examining the RQ.

When plants come into contact with suitable fungi in the soil in which they grow, they may form mycorrhizae. In a mycorrhizal association, the hyphae of the mycorrhiza provide a large surface area for the absorption of nutrient salts. This promotes the growth of plants that have formed mycorrhizae. Conversely, when seeds from another environment are planted in soil without suitable fungi, mycorrhizae are not formed and the plants may show deficiency of nutrients such as phosphate.

Garlic mustard (Allieaira petiolate), which invaded America from Europe, prevents native plants from forming mycorrhizae with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi through chemical components that it releases into the soil. In America, this alien plant has therefore expanded its range by suppressing the growth of other plants.

The membrane potential of a cell expresses the potential of the inside of the cell membrane taking the outside of the cell membrane as the reference (0 V). The cell membrane has K channels that are always open (leak K channels). Because the concentration of potassium ions (K⁺) in the cytoplasm is kept higher than outside the cell, K⁺ tends to flow out of the cell by diffusion. However, owing to differences between the inside and outside of the cell in the concentrations of ions that cannot pass freely through the cell membrane, and so on, the inside of the cell is negatively charged compared with the outside, so K⁺ tends to flow into the cell. Equilibrium is reached when the outflow and inflow balance. The membrane potential produced in this way is called the resting potential and is given by the following equation, using the K⁺ concentrations in the Nernst equation.

$$V\,(\mathrm{mV}) = 61.5 \log_{10}(C_{\mathrm{Ko}}/C_{\mathrm{Ki}})$$

Here, $C_{\mathrm{Ko}}$ is the extracellular concentration of K⁺ and $C_{\mathrm{Ki}}$ is the intracellular concentration of K⁺. (Note: $\log_{10} 100 = 2$, $\log_{10} 10 = 1$, $\log_{10} 1 = 0$, $\log_{10} 0.1 = -1$, $\log_{10} 0.01 = -2$)

The cell membrane also has many voltage-gated Na channels, which are closed at rest and open temporarily, for a very short time, in response to a voltage stimulus at or above the threshold. When a voltage stimulus at or above the threshold is applied, these voltage-gated Na channels open all at once (excitation). The amount of Na⁺ that moves in this state is very large compared with the amounts of K⁺ and other ions that move through various channels. As a result, a membrane potential that depends strongly on the Na⁺ concentration is produced. This is called the action potential and is observed as a pulse of 1 millisecond or less. Here, the membrane potential during this excitation is also considered to be determined approximately by the Nernst equation.

Haemoglobin, contained in the red blood cells of vertebrates, transports oxygen to the tissues by binding and releasing oxygen.

$$\mathrm{Hb}\ (\text{haemoglobin}) + \mathrm{O_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{HbO_2}\ (\text{oxyhaemoglobin})$$

In the alveoli, where the oxygen concentration is high, most of the haemoglobin binds oxygen and becomes oxyhaemoglobin; in the tissues, where the oxygen concentration is low, it releases oxygen readily, returns to haemoglobin and supplies oxygen to the tissues. The following model has been proposed for the diversity of species living on an island far from a continent.

The species diversity of an island is determined by the balance between the immigration rate of species from the continent (number of immigrating species per unit time) and the extinction rate of the species already established (number of species going extinct per unit time). The immigration rate is highest when there are no organisms at all on the island, and it decreases as the number of species living there increases. Each species may go extinct for various reasons, but, owing to effects such as interspecific competition, the extinction rate increases as the number of species increases. Species diversity, that is, the number of species living there, reaches an equilibrium when the immigration rate and the extinction rate become equal. In the figure, the point at which the immigration-rate line and the extinction-rate line cross indicates the equilibrium number of species on that island (Figure 1). The number of species is also strongly affected by the size of the island and by whether its distance from the continent is near or far (Figures 2 and 3).

The three-domain theory, which divides all living organisms into three groups, is generally accepted. The three groups are the archaea (archaebacteria), the bacteria (eubacteria) and the eukaryotes. When the phylogenetic relationships of these three groups are considered, a phylogenetic tree like that in Figure 1 is considered first. This tree does not show the common ancestor of all organisms (corresponding to the root of the tree); it is called an unrooted tree. Placing a root on this tree means considering the order in which the groups branched off from the common ancestor of all organisms, and there are three ways of placing the root, a–c in Figure 2. For example, placing the root at a in Figure 2 gives a rooted tree like that in Figure 3. The black circle in Figure 3 is the common ancestor of all organisms. Here, if it is assumed that the common ancestor had a nucleus, "loss of the nucleus" occurred twice, as in Figure 4. If, however, it is assumed that the common ancestor had no nucleus, "gain of the nucleus" occurred once. In the maximum parsimony method, one of the methods of constructing phylogenetic trees, a tree with fewer changes is considered to be closer to the true tree.

Lactose metabolism in Escherichia coli involves a mechanism called the lactose operon. The lactose operon consists of the "repressor gene", the "regulatory region consisting of the promoter and the operator" and the "three genes involved in lactose metabolism".

In the lactose operon, when there is no lactose in the cell, the repressor binds to the operator located upstream of the three genes, and the synthesis of the messenger RNA (mRNA) of the three genes is repressed. When lactose is present in the E. coli cell, the repressor can no longer bind to the operator, and mRNA synthesis begins. Transcription that is induced and occurs by such a mechanism is called "inducible transcription".

On the other hand, in the recessive mutation $i^{-}$ of the repressor gene $i^{+}$, no repressor can be produced, and mRNA comes to be synthesised whether or not lactose, the inducer, is present. Transcription that always takes place regardless of conditions in this way is called "constitutive transcription". In E. coli, a constitutive mutation $o^{C}$, which is dominant over the wild type of the operator ($o^{+}$) and synthesises mRNA even in the absence of lactose, has further been discovered.

In photosynthesis, electrons are passed from H₂O to NADP⁺ through the electron transport chain of the photosystems, producing O₂ and NADPH, and at the same time ATP is synthesised from ADP and inorganic phosphate by the energy of the H⁺ gradient formed between the thylakoid lumen and the stroma. Normally, about 3 molecules of ATP are synthesised in the electron transport that produces 2 molecules of NADPH from 2 molecules of H₂O.

The NADPH and ATP made in this way are used in the Calvin–Benson cycle to fix CO₂ and produce sugar. When sugar is made from 1 molecule of CO₂, 2 molecules of NADPH and 3 molecules of ATP are consumed. Therefore, when exactly 3 molecules of ATP are synthesised in the electron transport that produces 2 molecules of NADPH, that is, when NADPH : ATP = 2 : 3, these are used, with nothing left over or lacking, for the fixation of 1 molecule of CO₂ through to sugar production, so the reaction equation of the whole of photosynthesis, including carbon fixation, can simply be written as

$$\mathrm{CO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \frac{1}{6}\left(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\right) + \mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{O_2}$$

In this reaction equation, the compound produced by carbon fixation is converted into glucose and shown as (C₆H₁₂O₆). Also, the H₂O that acts as the electron donor in electron transport is shown on the left-hand side, distinguished from the H₂O entering and leaving in other reactions.

The figure schematically shows the blood circulatory system of an anuran amphibian (frog). The white circle represents the heart and the hatched ellipses represent capillaries. In this animal, the blood pumped out of the heart is divided into the pulmonary circulation and the systemic circulation, and the pulmonary circulation branches further into the pulmonary artery and the cutaneous artery. Of these, the blood that has gone to the lungs returns to the heart as the pulmonary vein, whereas the blood that has gone to the skin joins the veins of the systemic circulation and returns to the heart. When the animal is under water, the blood flow to the lungs, which become useless, is suppressed, but the blood flow to the skin is maintained, and oxygen can be taken up from the water through the skin.

Some plant organs show a bending response to particular stimuli. Such bending responses include tropisms, in which the direction of bending is determined by the direction of the stimulus, and nastic movements (nasties), in which the direction of bending is fixed regardless of the direction of the stimulus. Plant bending responses are classified into various types by combining the way the direction of bending is determined with the kind of stimulus that causes the bending.

Sundews (モウセンゴケ類) are a group of insectivorous plants that have glandular hairs covered with mucilage on the surface of their leaves. When a sundew leaf catches an insect in the mucilage, it bends so as to wrap around the insect and digests it inside. Experimental results

• When a living fruit fly was attached to the upper side of a leaf, the leaf bent towards it within a short time.
• When an intact dead fruit fly was attached to the upper side of a leaf, the leaf eventually bent towards it, but it took a long time before the bending occurred.
• When a crushed dead fruit fly was attached to the upper side of a leaf, the leaf bent towards it within a short time.
• When a small stone about the same size as a fruit fly was attached to the upper side of a leaf, no bending occurred.
• When the upper side of a leaf was rubbed with a brush, no bending occurred.

From studies of mutants and other work on the floral organs of Arabidopsis thaliana (シロイヌナズナ), the ABC model, which explains the mechanism by which floral organs are determined, has been proposed. In this ABC model, as shown in the figure, the floral meristem is divided, from the outside, into four regions: region 1 (sepals), region 2 (petals), region 3 (stamens) and region 4 (pistil). The floral organ of each region is then determined by the combination of genes acting in that region.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/biology-olympiads-bank/main/images/jbo-2021-1-6-fig1.png

The four regions of the floral meristem

Figure labels (Japanese → English): がく片 = sepal; 花弁 = petal; おしべ = stamen; めしべ = pistil.

The ABC model consists mainly of three rules.

Rule 1: A-class genes determine the development of sepals; A-class genes and B-class genes, of petals; B-class genes and C-class genes, of stamens; and C-class genes, of the pistil.

Rule 2: A-class genes and C-class genes repress each other's expression.

Rule 3: In addition to their role in determining the development of floral organs, C-class genes also suppress the function of the stem cells present in the floral meristem and promote the switch from indeterminate to determinate growth. Consequently, once the floral organs have been formed, the growth of floral organs stops there.

② Petals arise in region 1.

③ Leaves arise in region 1.

④ A pistil arises in region 1.

⑤ Development of pistils occurs repeatedly in region 4.

⑥ Development of secondary flowers (floral organs consisting of sepals and petals) occurs repeatedly in region 4.

Some biomolecules and drugs involved in life phenomena exist as enantiomers (also called mirror-image isomers, antipodes or optical isomers). Enantiomers are isomers that are mirror images of each other (a counterpart reflected in a mirror, or the relationship between the right and left hands), and are written as the D form and L form or the R form and S form. Whether the three-dimensional structure of a molecule gives rise to enantiomers depends on an "asymmetric carbon", to which four different atoms or groups of atoms are bonded. When biomolecules or drugs are synthesised chemically, they are often produced as a racemate (a mixture of enantiomers), but in living organisms sometimes only a particular enantiomer is produced. Also, when the physiological activities of enantiomers are compared, a particular enantiomer sometimes shows a higher activity.

Thalidomide was used in the 1950s as an anti-nausea drug and a sleeping drug for pregnant women, but its use was banned because it has severe teratogenicity for the foetus (it induces malformations of the limbs). Later it became clear that thalidomide is effective against intractable diseases such as Hansen's disease (leprosy) and multiple myeloma, and its use is now approved provided that strict regulations on its administration are observed.

Thalidomide exists as R and S enantiomers, and in 1979 it was reported that only the S form is teratogenic. On the other hand, it is known that R- or S-thalidomide administered into the body rapidly undergoes a change in its three-dimensional structure and becomes a racemate, so there was a contradiction as to why the result that only the S form is teratogenic had been obtained (the thalidomide paradox). Recent research has shown that, when the R and S forms of thalidomide are mixed, the two bind to each other to form a stable dimer, and the dimer has a lower solubility and is less easily absorbed into cells from the digestive tract or the blood. In another study, the protein to which thalidomide binds in the cell (cereblon) was identified, and it also became clear that teratogenicity arises because the function of cereblon changes when thalidomide is bound to it. Furthermore, analysis of the three-dimensional structure of the cereblon protein revealed the details of the binding sites and binding modes of R- and S-thalidomide.

The blood circulation of mammals is a double circulation, consisting of the pulmonary circulation, which runs from the right ventricle through the lungs and into the left atrium, and the systemic circulation, which runs from the left ventricle through the whole body and into the right atrium. In both, blood sent out from the heart branches from the aorta into arterioles, reaches the capillary bed of one organ, merges again to form veins and returns to the heart (Figure 10-1A). In the circulatory system of mammals this principle is broken in several places. There, the blood vessels that have formed a capillary bed in one organ merge again into a vessel with a vein-like structure, and then, without returning directly to the heart, form a capillary bed again and supply another organ (Figure 10-1B). A vein-like vessel linking two organs is called a portal vein. One of the portal veins that mammals have is found in the liver (Figure 10-2). In humans, the total blood volume is about 5 L, of which about 4.5 L is in the systemic circulation and about 0.5 L in the pulmonary circulation.

Diabetes, one of the representative lifestyle-related diseases, is a disease in which, for some reason, glucose homeostasis can no longer be maintained normally, and irreversible damage occurs in various organs of the whole body because a state of high blood glucose continues. One of its causes is a state in which, because of a decline in the function of the β cells, insulin is not secreted sufficiently even when the blood glucose level rises. For patients in this state there is a treatment in which insulin is injected subcutaneously after meals, when the blood glucose level is thought to be rising, to lower the blood glucose level. Subcutaneous injection is a technique in which the injection needle passes through the epithelial tissue and the drug is injected into the connective tissue beneath it. The drug injected into the connective tissue is gradually absorbed into the surrounding capillary beds, eventually merges into the vena cava, and after passing through the pulmonary circulation is sent out from the heart to the whole body. Because the transfer of the drug from the connective tissue to the capillary beds is gradual, a sharp rise in the blood concentration of the drug is less likely to occur than with, for example, intravenous injection, in which the drug is injected directly into a blood vessel.

Information transmission from one nerve cell to another takes place at sites called synapses. Of the three reaction temperatures set in ordinary PCR, if the primers are such that annealing occurs even at a sufficiently high temperature, the temperature setting can be reduced to two steps by making the annealing and extension temperatures the same.

On the other hand, the optimum annealing temperature in PCR is set with reference to the temperature at which the template DNA and the primers are equally in an equilibrium of dissociation and association. That is, even without passing through a temperature at which double-stranded DNA is completely denatured, at a temperature at which annealing could theoretically occur the double-helix structure of the template DNA is in an equilibrium of dissociation and association, and annealing of the template DNA and a primer can occur there in such a way that the primer takes the place of one of the DNA strands.

Considering these points, the possibility arises that in an artificial DNA amplification reaction even the heat-denaturation step of DNA could be eliminated and the whole temperature setting fixed at a single step. However, when the DNA polymerase has the property shown in Figure 3-1 (A), even if a primer binds to the template DNA, the DNA extension reaction does not proceed when a strand that blocks the DNA extension reaction is already bound ahead of it (that is, as in the heat-denaturation step of PCR, the DNA extension reaction does not proceed unless there is a step in which the DNA clearly becomes single-stranded). On the other hand, with a DNA polymerase with the property of Figure 3-1 (B), the DNA extension reaction continues while the DNA strand already present is dissociated. A DNA polymerase with the property of Figure 3-1 (B) is called a strand-displacing DNA polymerase, but most of the DNA polymerases used in ordinary PCR have the property of Figure 3-1 (A).

In the flagellum, the dynein arms are thought to make the microtubules slide against each other using the energy released when they hydrolyse ATP, and the displacement produced then generates the bending. In that case, it is inferred that the reaction rate at which ATP is hydrolysed is almost proportional to the sliding velocity of the microtubules, and that this, provided the waveform does not change, is almost proportional to the beat frequency of the flagellum. The reaction should then be expressed by the reaction scheme below, so the Michaelis–Menten equation is thought to hold.

$$\mathrm{D} + \mathrm{ATP} \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_{+1}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \mathrm{D{\cdot}ATP} \xrightarrow{k_{+2}} \mathrm{D} + \mathrm{ADP} + \mathrm{P}i$$

Here D represents the dynein arm, P$i$ inorganic phosphate, and the k are reaction rate constants. D·ATP represents the complex of the dynein arm and ATP. The reaction between the dynein arms and the microtubules is not considered here.

If this reaction is taking place, then, treating the beat frequency f of the flagellum as the reaction rate and writing the ATP concentration as [ATP], there should be the following relationship between the frequency f and the ATP concentration.

$$\mathrm{f} = \frac{k_{+2}([\mathrm{D}] + [\mathrm{D{\cdot}ATP}])\,[\mathrm{ATP}]}{\dfrac{k_{-1} + k_{+2}}{k_{+1}} + [\mathrm{ATP}]}$$

Here, setting

$$\mathrm{fm}\ (\text{maximum frequency}) = k_{+2}([\mathrm{D}] + [\mathrm{D{\cdot}ATP}])$$

$$\mathrm{Km}\ (\text{Michaelis constant}) = \frac{k_{-1} + k_{+2}}{k_{+1}}$$

we obtain

$$\mathrm{f} = \frac{\mathrm{fm}\,[\mathrm{ATP}]}{\mathrm{Km} + [\mathrm{ATP}]} \qquad \text{(Michaelis–Menten equation)}$$

Rearranging this equation, $\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}}$, the reciprocal of the frequency f, is expressed as a linear function of $\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{ATP}]}$, the reciprocal of the ATP concentration, as follows.

$$\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}} = \frac{\mathrm{Km}}{\mathrm{fm}} \cdot \frac{1}{[\mathrm{ATP}]} + \frac{1}{\mathrm{fm}}$$

To confirm this, sea-urchin sperm whose cell membranes had been removed and that had been activated with ATP were observed under stroboscopic illumination, and the beat frequency of the flagella was measured at different ATP concentrations. Even when the ATP concentration was changed, the waveform of the flagella hardly changed and the frequency changed depending on the ATP concentration, so the frequencies were recorded; the result, with $\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{f}}$ on the vertical axis and $\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{ATP}]}$ on the horizontal axis, is Figure 10-1.

Even in organisms regarded as the same species, various variations between populations are seen in their characteristics. For example, the body size of insects with $\fbox{65}$ can change linearly with the mean annual temperature of their habitat. Populations living in cold environments tend to have a body size that is $\fbox{66}$, and populations living in warm environments one that is $\fbox{67}$.

Bodily development is, in the final analysis, chemical reactions (enzyme reactions, etc.), and requires temperatures above a certain level. Insects, being ectotherms, cannot produce heat themselves, so they obtain the heat energy needed for development from the outside (air temperature, etc.). Developing a $\fbox{68}$ body requires a large amount of heat, and the developmental time becomes longer. In cold environments the period during which temperatures allowing development are reached is short, and $\fbox{69}$ individuals are at a disadvantage in development, for example their growth is delayed; through natural selection, therefore, $\fbox{70}$ individuals survive more easily and leave more offspring (genes). However, by this explanation alone, there would be no problem with there being $\fbox{71}$ individuals in warm environments.

What should be looked at next is the relationship between body size and the number of offspring. In taxa in which, as in insects, a female produces many eggs at a time, the more $\fbox{72}$ a female is, the more eggs she can produce. If there are small females and large females in a warm environment, the $\fbox{73}$ females will have more offspring and are expected to leave more genes to the next generation.

In summary, such patterns of geographical variation in body size are explained as arising because body-size variation has a genetic basis and the number of offspring is maximised within the season in which development is possible.

Absorbance is defined as follows.

When light passes through a light-absorbing substance, the light is absorbed and its intensity decreases. Using the intensity $I_0$ of the irradiated light of a particular wavelength and the intensity $I$ of the transmitted light, the transmittance $T$ is defined by

$$T = \frac{I}{I_0}$$

In actual measurements, if the transmitted light becomes too weak it cannot be measured accurately, and $T$ needs to be at least about 0.01 (1%). The logarithm of the reciprocal of $T$ is the absorbance $A$:

$$A = \log_{10}\frac{I_0}{I} = -\log_{10}\frac{I}{I_0} = -\log_{10}T$$

For a particular substance, the following relationship holds (the Lambert–Beer law).

$$A = K \times c \times l$$

[where $K$: a constant for each substance and wavelength, $c$: concentration of the substance, $l$: optical path length (the length of the substance through which the light passes)]

Here, $K$ at a concentration of 1 mol/L and an optical path length of 1 cm is called the molar absorption coefficient and is denoted by ε. That is, the vertical axis of the graph shows the absorbance $A$ per 1 mmol/L of concentration and per 1 cm of optical path length. The genetic information of organisms is represented by the sequence of the four kinds of bases contained in DNA [adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T)]. One of the methods for determining a base sequence is the Sanger method.

In the Sanger method, a single strand of the DNA to be analysed is used as the template, and DNA fragments are synthesised in a reaction mixture containing one kind of primer that binds specifically to the template DNA, eight kinds of nucleotides (four kinds of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates and four kinds of dideoxyribonucleoside triphosphates) and DNA polymerase. The dideoxyribonucleoside triphosphates are labelled with fluorescence of a different colour for each of the four bases (A: red, C: yellow, G: green, T: blue), and when one of them is incorporated into the growing new DNA strand, elongation of that strand stops. The synthesised single-stranded DNA is subjected to agarose gel electrophoresis with fluorescence detection, and the base sequence is read from the pattern of the bands obtained.

The mark–recapture method is one of the methods for estimating the number of individuals in a population. The basic procedure of this method is as follows. $m$ individuals are captured at random from the population, marked and returned to the original population (first capture). After a certain period, $c$ individuals are captured at random from the population, and $r$ of them are found to be marked (second capture). The number of individuals in the population ($N$) is estimated from the relation $N : m = c : r$ as

$$N = \frac{mc}{r} \qquad (1)$$

In Japan, seasonal influenza spreads every winter. The main symptoms of influenza are fever of 38 °C or higher, joint and muscle pain, general fatigue, headache, runny or blocked nose, sneezing, cough and sore throat; when there are symptoms such as a high fever suggesting influenza, (ア) rapid tests are carried out, for example at fever outpatient clinics.

The causative virus, the influenza virus, is mainly classified into types A, B and C, of which types A and B cause major epidemics. As shown in Figure 1, these types are covered by an envelope made of a lipid bilayer, and on its surface they have the proteins haemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). HA binds to a sugar called sialic acid on the surface of the host cell and enables the virus to enter the cell, while NA has the function of cutting off sialic acid when the virus leaves an infected cell. (イ) According to differences in HA and NA, type A viruses are further divided into several subtypes.

For an enzyme, with reaction rate $v$ and substrate concentration [S], the basic equation of enzyme kinetics is expressed as

$$v = \frac{V_{\mathrm{max}}[\mathrm{S}]}{K_{\mathrm{m}} + [\mathrm{S}]} \quad \cdots \quad \text{(エ)}$$

$V_{\mathrm{max}}$ in the equation is the maximum reaction rate. $K_{\mathrm{m}}$ is called the Michaelis constant and corresponds to the substrate concentration at which the rate is $\frac{1}{2}V_{\mathrm{max}}$.

When the relationship between the reaction rate of an enzyme and the substrate concentration is determined experimentally by measuring the enzyme activity at various substrate concentrations, and the results are plotted with the substrate concentration on the horizontal axis and the enzyme activity on the vertical axis, the plot takes the shape of curve (オ) in Figure 3. When an inhibitor such as oseltamivir is added to such an experimental system, the plot changes from curve (オ) to curve (カ).
